Your body's ancient survival system and why it sometimes misfires.

Your nervous system has a built-in alarm system designed to keep you alive. When it detects danger, it triggers one of three responses: fight, flight, or freeze. This system hasn't changed much since our ancestors faced physical threats like predators.

Fight: Increased aggression, tension, urge to confront

Flight: Urge to escape, restlessness, anxiety

Freeze: Feeling stuck, unable to think or move, dissociation

All three are your body's attempt to protect you.

Your brain can't distinguish between a physical threat (a predator) and a psychological one (an angry email from your boss). Both trigger the same survival response, flooding your body with stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline.
Recognising which response you tend toward helps you manage it. Do you get angry? Want to run? Or do you shut down?

Things that can help you feel calmer after a stress response:

• Physical activity, even a short walk
• Calming breathing exercises
• Talking to someone you trust

These are all on the NHS list of things that can help with stress.

Understanding neuroplasticity and why it's never too late to rewire your thinking.

For decades, scientists believed the adult brain was fixed and unchangeable. We now know this is completely wrong. Your brain is constantly rewiring itself based on your experiences, thoughts, and behaviours. This is called neuroplasticity.

Think of your brain like paths in a forest. The paths you walk most often become clear and easy to travel. Paths you ignore become overgrown. Your thoughts work the same way - repeated thoughts strengthen neural pathways, making them easier to access.

This means:

• Negative thought patterns can be unlearned
• New, healthier patterns can be built
• It takes repetition and consistency
• Change is possible at any age
Every time you choose a different response to a familiar trigger, you're literally rewiring your brain.

To change a pattern:

1. Become aware of the existing pattern
2. Deliberately choose a different response
3. Repeat consistently over time

New habits take time to become automatic, often a couple of months or more. Keep going even when it feels slow.

Why sleep is not a luxury but a necessity for mental wellbeing.

Sleep isn't just rest for your body - it's essential maintenance time for your brain. During sleep, your brain processes emotions, consolidates memories, and clears out toxins that build up during waking hours.

REM sleep (when we dream) is crucial for emotional processing. Your brain essentially "reviews" the day's emotional experiences and files them properly. Without enough REM sleep, emotions stay raw and unprocessed.

Sleep and mood are closely linked. The NHS notes that low mood can cause problems sleeping, and that getting more sleep is one of the small changes that can help low mood. When you are short of sleep, it is often harder to cope with stress.
If you're feeling emotionally volatile, ask yourself: "How did I sleep last night?"

Key factors for better sleep:

• Consistent wake time (even weekends)
• Limited screen time before bed
• Cool, dark environment
• No caffeine after early afternoon
• Wind-down routine

Think of emotions as messengers, not problems:

• Fear alerts you to potential danger
• Sadness signals loss or unmet needs

The emotion itself isn't the problem - it's information.
Many of us learned to judge our emotions: "I shouldn't feel this way" or "I'm being stupid." This judgement adds suffering on top of the original feeling. You end up feeling bad about feeling bad.
Try replacing "I shouldn't feel this" with "It makes sense I feel this because..."

Validating an emotion doesn't mean the emotion is "right" or that you should act on it. It simply means acknowledging that the feeling exists and has a reason.

Learning to observe your thoughts without believing everything they tell you.

Your mind produces thousands of thoughts every day. Many of these thoughts are automatic - they pop up without your conscious choice. Just because a thought appears in your mind doesn't make it true or important.

Your brain is a prediction machine, constantly generating thoughts about what might happen, what could go wrong, and what things mean. Many of these predictions are based on past experiences and may not apply to current situations.

Watch out for these patterns:

• All-or-nothing thinking: "If it's not perfect, it's a failure"
• Mind reading: "They must think I'm an idiot"
• Fortune telling: "This will definitely go wrong"
• Catastrophising: "This is the worst thing ever"

These are common but often inaccurate.
When you notice a strong negative thought, ask: "Is this a fact or an interpretation?"
Instead of "I'm a failure," try "I'm having the thought that I'm a failure." This small shift creates distance between you and the thought, making it easier to question its accuracy.

Anger is a normal emotion. Here's how to spot it early and stop it running the show.

Everyone gets angry sometimes. It's a normal human emotion, and on its own it isn't a problem. It becomes a problem when it starts to damage your relationships, your work or how you feel about yourself.

Anger affects your body, your mind and what you do. You might notice:

• Body: heart beating faster, tight muscles, clenched fists, a tight chest, feeling hot
• Mind: feeling tense or on edge, unable to relax, irritable, humiliated or resentful
• Behaviour: shouting, sulking or ignoring people, starting fights, breaking things

Some people turn anger inwards instead, which can show up as self-harm. It isn't always obvious that anger is behind a change in how you're acting.

What sets anger off is different for everyone, but common triggers include:

• Being treated unfairly and feeling powerless to change it
• Feeling threatened or attacked
• People not respecting your feelings or your things
• Being stopped from getting something done

You're more likely to react strongly when you're already stressed, when you've been through trauma, or when alcohol or drugs are involved. How the adults around you handled anger when you were growing up can play a part too.

• Pause before you react. Count to 10 or take a few slow breaths
• Practise noticing your body's early warning signs so you can step away sooner
• Talk it through with someone who isn't involved
• Get moving. Walking, running, swimming or yoga all help burn off tension
• Set small, realistic goals rather than trying to fix everything at once
• Put your energy into what you can change, not what you can't

• Mind: feeling tense, unable to relax, worrying about the past or future, poor sleep, struggling to concentrate, fearing the worst

Good relationships with partners, friends and family are one of the most important things for your mental health. Healthy relationships don't just happen. They take effort from everyone involved.

You can often tell a relationship is healthy by how it makes you feel:

• You feel safe, and your boundaries are respected
• Differences are expected and can be talked about openly
• You can be yourself without hiding parts of who you are
• You can say how you feel without the other person having to guess

Respect, honesty, trust and good communication are the foundations.

Understanding your own feelings makes it easier to explain them to someone else. If you struggle to name or manage your emotions, that can spill over into your relationships.

Anger, for example, often sits on top of hurt or upset. Recognising that, and saying it, can bring you closer rather than pushing people away.

Boundaries aren't only about what you don't want. They're also about telling people what you value. Let others know your limits, like needing time to yourself after a long shift. Clear boundaries take the pressure off trying to meet expectations nobody can live up to.

Disagreements happen in every relationship. What matters is how you talk to each other.

• Raise small issues early, before they build up
• Use "I" statements: "When X happens, I feel Y"
• Pick a good time to talk, not in the middle of something else
• Listen to understand, not to plan your reply
• Repeat back what you heard so they know you've got it
Talking while walking or driving side by side can make difficult conversations feel less intense.

You can only control your own actions, not anyone else's. Accepting that saves a lot of energy and stress. Think about which of your relationships work best, what makes them work, and how you could bring more of that into others.

Every couple disagrees. Arguing isn't a sign your relationship is failing, but if the same arguments keep happening or keep getting heated, it's worth looking at how you handle them.

Some ways of talking almost guarantee a row:

• Accusations like "You don't care" put people on the defensive
• Words like "always" and "never" exaggerate the problem
• Bringing up old arguments drags you off topic

Try describing your own experience instead: "I feel left out when plans change last minute." Stick to one issue at a time.

If things are escalating, take a break. Walking away can feel like losing, but it puts the relationship ahead of being right. Say briefly why you're stopping and when you'd like to pick it up again.

Watch for signs in your body, like a racing heart or clenched jaw. They're a cue to pause.
Slow, deep breaths help calm your body down before you go back to the conversation.

The thing you're arguing about is often not the real issue. A row about someone always being late might really be about feeling disrespected or unheard. If you're far angrier than the situation seems to deserve, there's probably something bigger underneath. Talking about that can help you both.

When you're both calm, agree how you'll handle disagreements:

• Listen to each other and look for compromise
• No shouting or name-calling
• Don't argue in front of the children
• Agree a signal for taking a break
• Once it's resolved, let it go and start fresh

• Damages your belongings

Grief is what we feel when we lose something or someone important. That could be a death, but it can also be the end of a relationship, losing a job, leaving a career or moving away from home.

• Shock or numbness, like being in a daze
• Overwhelming sadness and lots of crying
• Exhaustion
• Anger, at the person, the situation or yourself
• Guilt about things said or not said, or that you couldn't stop it

Grief can feel chaotic, but for most people it becomes less intense over time.

• Talk about how you feel with someone you trust
• Connect with others who have been through a similar loss
• Keep moving. Regular exercise helps mood and sleep
• Eat regular meals to keep your energy up
• Set small goals rather than trying to do everything
• Avoid using alcohol or drugs to numb the pain

Service Family Accommodation is heavily subsidised. The equivalent rent in many areas would be £800–£1,200 per month. And with FHTB, getting on the property ladder is within reach.
Free gym access, sports facilities, and paid time to exercise. A civilian gym membership alone costs £40–£80 per month.
You get 38 days of leave a year. By law, most full-time workers are entitled to at least 28 days (including bank holidays).
In uncertain economic times, military careers offer a level of job security that most industries simply cannot match.
Clear, structured promotion pathways. You know exactly what you need to do to progress — no office politics.
A built-in support network wherever you go. The friendships and bonds formed in service last a lifetime.
The Career Transition Partnership helps you find civilian work with CV workshops, training, and job matching.
HIVE information services, welfare support, childcare vouchers, and family activity centres on most bases.

Healthy relationships are built on a foundation of trust. This means feeling safe to be yourself, knowing your partner will be honest, and believing they have your best interests at heart. Trust takes time to build and requires consistent actions, not just words.
You deserve relationships where you feel safe.

Good communication isn't about never disagreeing - it's about how you handle differences. Healthy couples can express needs, listen actively, and work through conflict without contempt or stonewalling. It's a skill that can be learned.
Every conversation is a chance to connect.

Respect means valuing your partner's feelings, opinions, and boundaries - even when you disagree. It means not trying to control or change them. Healthy boundaries protect both people and actually bring you closer.
Boundaries are an act of love, not rejection.

The healthiest relationships balance closeness with individuality. You can be deeply connected while still having your own friends, interests, and identity. Needing space doesn't mean you love each other less.
You can be fully yourself and fully loved.

Passive communicators often avoid expressing their needs or opinions to keep the peace. They may say "it's fine" when it isn't, then feel resentful. This style often comes from learning that your needs weren't important or would cause conflict.

Aggressive communication prioritises your needs over others, often through criticism, blame, or intimidation. It usually comes from a place of fear or hurt, not strength. It damages trust and pushes people away.

This indirect style expresses negative feelings through actions rather than words - the silent treatment, sarcasm, or "forgetting" to do things. It often develops when direct expression didn't feel safe.
It's okay to say what you need directly.

Assertive communication expresses your needs clearly and respectfully while considering others. It sounds like "I feel..." rather than "You always...". This is the healthiest style and can be learned with practice.
You can be honest and kind at the same time.

Some people feel most loved when they hear it expressed in words - compliments, encouragement, "I love you", or acknowledgment of what they do. If this is your language, silence can feel like rejection even when it's not meant that way.
Your need to hear love spoken is valid.

For some, actions speak louder than words. Helping with tasks, taking care of things, or easing someone's burden shows love. If this is your language, a partner who doesn't help may feel uncaring, even if they express love in other ways.
Noticing what someone does is love in itself.

Undivided attention, being fully present, doing things together - this is how some people feel most connected. Distractions or cancelled plans can feel deeply personal. It's not about quantity, but about presence.
Hugs, holding hands, physical closeness - for some, this is how love feels real. If this is your language, physical distance (even if unintentional) can make you feel unloved or disconnected.

Thoughtful gifts, big or small, represent love and consideration to some people. It's not about materialism - it's about someone thinking of you. A forgotten birthday might hurt more deeply than others understand.
It's the thought behind the gift that matters.
Think about what makes you feel safe in a relationship. Is it consistency? Honesty? Knowing they'll be there?
When do you feel most secure with someone? What creates that feeling?
Consider how you like to communicate in relationships. Do you need to talk things through immediately, or do you prefer time to process?
How do you prefer to handle disagreements? Have past partners matched this?
Think about the balance between togetherness and personal space that works for you.
How much time alone do you need to feel like yourself? Is this respected in your relationships?
Consider what you want your life to look like - where you live, family, career, lifestyle.
Are your core life goals compatible with your partner's? Have you discussed them?
Sometimes we find ourselves in similar relationships or situations repeatedly. This isn't bad luck - it's often a pattern worth understanding.
Is there a type of person you're drawn to? A dynamic that keeps appearing? What might this be about?
We often take on certain roles in relationships - the caretaker, the fixer, the one who gives in. These roles may have developed for good reasons, but they can limit us.
What role do you tend to play in relationships? Is this the role you want?
How relationships end can reveal patterns too. Do you tend to leave first, stay too long, or push people away?
Looking back at relationships that ended, do you notice any patterns in how or why they ended?
Instead of "You never listen to me," try "I feel unheard when I'm interrupted." This expresses your experience without triggering defensiveness.
Notice when you're about to say "You always" or "You never"
Pause and rephrase as "I feel... when..."
Focus on the specific situation, not character attacks
Speaking your truth can be gentle.
Active listening means trying to understand, not just waiting for your turn to speak. Put down distractions, make eye contact, and reflect back what you hear.
When your partner speaks, focus fully on them
Don't plan your response while they're talking
Say "What I'm hearing is..." to check understanding
Being truly heard is a gift you can give.
When emotions run high, it is hard to think clearly. Taking a short break, agreed with your partner, with a promise to come back to the conversation, can stop things you'll regret being said.
Learn to recognise when you're "flooded" (racing heart, can't think clearly)
Agree on a signal with your partner (e.g., "I need a few minutes")
Use the break to calm down, not to rehearse arguments
Always return to the conversation when ready
Boundaries start with knowing what you can and can't accept. This requires tuning into your own feelings and taking them seriously.
Notice what makes you feel uncomfortable or resentful
These feelings are signals about your boundaries
Write down your non-negotiables in relationships
State boundaries clearly and calmly: "I'm not comfortable with..." or "I need...". You don't need to justify or over-explain.
You can be firm and loving.
Setting a boundary once isn't enough. You may need to remind, reinforce, or follow through with consequences if boundaries are repeatedly crossed.
Expect some pushback - it doesn't mean you're wrong
Have clear consequences and follow through
What feelings are trying to tell you

Every emotion you feel has a purpose. Anger signals a boundary has been crossed. Fear alerts you to potential danger. Sadness tells you something is lost. Rather than fighting your feelings, try understanding what they're telling you.

Often what we show on the surface (anger, irritation) is covering a deeper feeling (hurt, fear, rejection). Many people, especially men, were taught to express anger but not vulnerability. Understanding your primary emotion helps you address the real issue.
It's okay to feel what's underneath.

We all have emotional patterns shaped by our past. Maybe you shut down when criticised, or get anxious when plans change. These patterns made sense once - they were your way of coping. Understanding them gives you choice.

Many men were taught to hold it together, push through, and not show pain. That strength helped you survive - but survival isn't the same as living well. What we don't express doesn't disappear; it settles into stress, tension, and distance from those we care about.
You matter. What you feel matters.

Opening up doesn't mean losing control or falling apart. It means being human. Talking is not weakness - it's maintenance. You don't need perfect words or a full story. Start small. One honest moment. One trusted person.
Real strength isn't pretending nothing hurts.

Many men want the same things as everyone else: to feel respected and not belittled. Appreciation — to know their actions and feelings are seen. Emotional safety — a space with no judgement. Desire — to feel wanted. To matter — to know their presence makes a difference. Acceptance — being loved for exactly who they are, not what they provide.

Autonomy — the space to make choices and feel trusted. Permission to feel — even if you don't always know how to express emotions, having the space to try without judgement. And peace — less chaos, less criticism, calm environments. These aren't luxuries. They're what allows a man to be present, open, and connected.
Needing peace is not the same as avoiding life.

During your period, oestrogen and progesterone are at their lowest. Your body is shedding the uterine lining and energy naturally dips. Some women feel tired, have cramps, or notice lower mood during their period. Everyone is different, and your experience may change from month to month.
Rest, comfort, patience, and reduced demands
A warm water bottle or gentle stretching can help with cramps
Speak to your GP if period pain stops you doing everyday things
After your period, oestrogen starts rising. Some women notice they feel more energetic in the days after their period ends, but this varies a lot from person to person.
Notice how you feel across the month — your own pattern matters more than any rule
A simple diary can help you spot patterns
Regular exercise is good for your mood at any point in your cycle
Around the middle of your cycle, an egg is released from an ovary. Some women notice mild one-sided pain or a change in vaginal discharge around this time.
Mild mid-cycle pain is common and usually harmless
See your GP if pain is severe or does not settle
Trust what your body is telling you

In the days before a period, many women get premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Symptoms can include mood swings, feeling irritable or anxious, tiredness, bloating and breast tenderness. They usually ease once your period starts.
Regular exercise, enough sleep and a healthy, balanced diet can help PMS (NHS)
Keep a diary of symptoms for at least 2 menstrual cycles
See your GP if PMS affects your daily life
Your feelings are real, and they will shift.

Feeling secure enough to express emotions without them being dismissed, minimised, or used against you. A relationship where you can be vulnerable without fear. This is the foundation everything else is built on.
You deserve to feel safe being yourself.
Words and actions that align. Knowing someone will show up — not just on the good days. Consistency isn't about grand gestures; it's about the small, reliable things that build trust over time.
You deserve someone whose actions match their words.

The effort to listen, to try to understand, and to talk through issues calmly rather than shutting down or exploding. Communication isn't about agreeing on everything — it's about being willing to try.
Emotional and physical closeness — not just in the good times. A hand held during a hard day. A hug that says "I'm here." Affection isn't a luxury; it's how many women feel connected and valued.
Not just looked at — truly seen. Noticed when something is wrong. Appreciated for the invisible work you do. Acknowledged as a whole person, not just a role you fill.
You are more than what you do for others.
Being supportive means being present — not avoidant or detached when things get difficult. It means leaning in, not pulling away. Being willing to sit in discomfort together.
You deserve someone who stays in the room.

Encouragement to evolve and pursue purpose. A partner who celebrates your ambition rather than feeling threatened by it. Growth isn't about changing who you are — it's about becoming more of who you are.
Your growth is not a threat to the right person.
Loving what you have and not lusting over what you don't have. Feeling chosen — not settled for. Knowing your partner sees you, appreciates you, and isn't constantly looking elsewhere.
You are enough. Right now. As you are.
How to train smarter with your body
Exercise can help with period pain. Some women prefer lighter sessions during their period and others train as normal. Listen to your body.
Walking, swimming, or gentle yoga can ease cramps
Train as normal if you feel well
Rest if you need to — recovery is part of training

Women respond differently across their cycle. Some notice their energy and performance change; many notice no difference. Tracking how training feels alongside your cycle helps you learn what is true for you.
Note energy, sleep and how sessions feel
Look for your own patterns over a few months
Adjust training based on how you feel, not a fixed rule
Your body is built for this.
A good warm-up, sensible progression and enough recovery protect you from injury at every point in your cycle.
Warm up thoroughly before every session
Get help early for any pain that does not settle
If you get PMS, the NHS says regular exercise can help ease symptoms. Some women find sessions feel harder in the days before their period; if so, that is normal and temporary.
Keep moving — regular exercise can help PMS
Don't judge your fitness by one hard week
The transition nobody warns you about

Perimenopause is the transition period before menopause, often starting in your mid-to-late 40s but sometimes earlier. Hormone levels become unpredictable — oestrogen can spike and crash rather than gradually declining. Many women are blindsided because nobody told them this was coming.

Irregular periods, hot flushes, night sweats, brain fog, anxiety (often sudden and unexplained), joint pain, fatigue, sleep disruption, mood swings, rage, low libido, weight changes, and heart palpitations. These are frequently misdiagnosed as stress, anxiety disorders, or depression — especially in high-pressure military environments.
Track your symptoms — patterns help your doctor diagnose
Ask your GP or MO specifically about perimenopause
Don't accept "it's just stress" if symptoms don't add up
You are not losing your mind. Your hormones are shifting.

HRT (hormone replacement therapy) can relieve many symptoms. It has benefits and some risks, so talk them through with your GP or MO to decide what is right for you. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) can help with mood symptoms. Exercise, sleep hygiene, and reducing alcohol also make a significant difference. You should not have to suffer in silence — this is a medical condition, not a weakness.
Speak to your GP or MO — ask directly about HRT options
Keep a symptom diary for at least 3 months
Connect with other women going through it — you are not alone
When your luteal phase becomes unbearable

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a very severe form of PMS. It causes strong emotional and physical symptoms in the 1 to 2 weeks before a period. Symptoms include severe depression, rage, hopelessness, anxiety, and in some cases suicidal thoughts — that lift almost immediately once your period starts.
If this sounds familiar, you are not broken.

The hallmark of PMDD is the pattern: severe symptoms in the 1-2 weeks before your period that disappear within a few days of bleeding starting. If you track your mood against your cycle and see this pattern repeating, speak to your doctor. A GP usually needs to see your symptoms recorded over at least 2 cycles to diagnose PMDD.
Track mood daily alongside your cycle for 2-3 months
Note when symptoms start and when they lift
Show your doctor the pattern — it's the key to diagnosis
Naming it is the first step to managing it.

PMDD is treatable. Your GP can talk you through options, which may include lifestyle changes, talking therapy such as CBT, antidepressants or hormonal treatment. Many women find dramatic improvement once they get the right support. You do not have to white-knuckle through every month.
There is help. You deserve it.
Why you might be running on empty

Heavy periods are the most common cause of iron deficiency in women. Low iron means less oxygen reaches your muscles and brain. The result: persistent fatigue, dizziness, breathlessness on exertion, brain fog, and reduced physical performance. Many active women attribute this to overtraining or stress when the real issue is their iron levels.

Unusual tiredness that rest doesn't fix. Feeling breathless during exercise that used to be manageable. Pale skin, brittle nails, feeling cold. Difficulty concentrating. Craving ice or non-food items (pica). If you're experiencing these alongside heavy periods, speak to your GP. A simple blood test can check for iron deficiency anaemia.
See your GP — a blood test can check your iron levels
Iron-rich foods: red meat, spinach, lentils, fortified cereals
Vitamin C helps iron absorption — pair with meals
Your body is trying to tell you something.
Pain that deserves to be taken seriously

Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the womb — on the ovaries, bowel, or elsewhere in the pelvis. It is a common condition. Symptoms include severe period pain, chronic pelvic pain, pain during or after sex, fatigue, and difficulty getting pregnant. It can take a long time to diagnose, so keep asking for help if your pain is affecting your life.
Pain that stops you functioning is never "just a period".

Service women with endometriosis often push through pain to avoid being seen as weak or unreliable. Getting checked early means you can get support to manage symptoms. If period pain regularly affects your ability to train, work, or sleep — that is not normal and you deserve investigation. Treatments include hormonal management, pain relief, and in some cases surgery.
Keep a pain diary — note severity, timing, and impact on duties
Ask your MO for a referral to gynaecology if pain is severe
Hormonal contraception can sometimes help manage symptoms
Advocating for your health is not weakness.

Many service women choose to suppress periods before and during deployment using hormonal contraception. This is medically safe and widely used. The combined pill taken back-to-back, the hormonal IUD, the implant, or the injection can all reduce or eliminate periods. Speak to your MO well before deployment to find what works for your body — don't leave it to the last minute.
Discuss options with your MO at least 3 months before deployment
Trial the method at home first to check for side effects
Carry backup supplies (panty liners, painkillers) regardless
Planning ahead is professionalism, not weakness.

When periods happen on exercise or operations: menstrual cups are popular because they're reusable and last up to 12 hours. Period pants work well as backup. Carry disposal bags (opaque, sealable) for used products. Baby wipes for hygiene when showers aren't available. Anti-diarrhoea medication (Imodium) can help if bowel changes accompany your period.
Practice using a menstrual cup before you need it in the field
Pack supplies in your grab bag — not in a bergen that might get separated
Dark-coloured underwear gives peace of mind
Every woman who has served has figured this out. You will too.

Extended time away from loved ones takes a psychological toll. Isolation can lead to overthinking, low mood, sleep disruption, and relationship strain. Recognising these as normal responses helps you manage them.
This is temporary. One day at a time.

When you're isolated, structure becomes your anchor. Consistent wake times, regular exercise, and small rituals provide psychological stability. Even small routines - a morning coffee, an evening wind-down - help.
Set consistent wake and sleep times
Create something to look forward to each day

Leaving the military isn't just changing jobs - it's leaving behind an identity, a community, a way of life. Feeling lost, uncertain, or grieving what you've left is completely normal. Give yourself time to find who you are outside the uniform.
Who you are is bigger than any role.

Civilian life can feel slower, less purposeful, or frustrating. The clear hierarchy and mission focus of military life is replaced by ambiguity. This adjustment takes time - often more than people expect.
It takes time to find your new rhythm.

Being alongside someone in the military is its own challenge. The worry, the separations, the uncertainty, managing life alone during deployments - your experience is valid. You don't need to minimise what you go through.
You're not "just" supporting - you're carrying too.
Reunions aren't always smooth. They've changed, you've changed, and it takes time to reconnect. Give each other grace. The person who left isn't exactly the person who returns, and that's okay.
Reconnection takes patience from both sides.
If you're having thoughts of ending your life, please reach out now. You don't have to face this alone. These feelings are temporary, even though they don't feel that way right now.
If you are in immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E
NHS 111, mental health option: urgent help, 24/7
Text SHOUT to 85258 for text support (24/7)
Veterans and serving personnel can also call the Combat Stress helpline on 0800 138 1619 (24/7) for mental health support
If you're experiencing domestic abuse or feel unsafe, help is available. You deserve to be safe.

NHS: signs of autism in adults

Neurodiversity is the idea that brains work in different ways, and that these differences should be recognised and respected like any other human difference. Someone whose brain works differently from most people may describe themselves as neurodivergent.
Autism and ADHD are often described as types of neurodivergence.
Specific learning difficulties (SpLDs), such as dyslexia, dyspraxia and dyscalculia, are also part of neurodiversity.
These conditions often overlap. For example, ADHD is more common in autistic people, and dyspraxia often occurs alongside ADHD, dyslexia or autism.
These terms sound alike but mean different things.
A specific learning difficulty, such as dyslexia, affects particular skills like reading, writing or working with numbers. It does not affect intelligence.

A learning disability affects the way a person learns new things throughout their life, and can affect understanding complicated information or looking after yourself. Many people with a learning disability work, have relationships and live independently.
Some autistic people have a learning disability, and many do not.

Autism is not an illness. It is something you are born with, and so is dyspraxia. Dyslexia is a difference in how your brain works and does not affect intelligence. There is no cure for these conditions, but there are ways to manage the difficulties and get support.
People with ADHD, autism or dyspraxia are more likely to have mental health problems such as anxiety and depression. ADHD is also linked to a higher risk of suicide.
If you feel like ending your life, tell someone and get help straight away.
See the Suicide Awareness section of this app, or call Samaritans free on 116 123.

Autism is a difference in how your brain develops. It can change how you communicate, learn and pay attention, and how you react to things like light, sound, smell, taste and touch. The medical name for a diagnosis is autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
Finding it hard to talk with other people, or preferring to spend time alone.
Finding it hard to read facial expressions, gestures or tone of voice.
Taking things literally, for example not understanding some sayings or figures of speech.
Having fixed routines and getting upset if they change.
A very strong interest in particular subjects.
Being very sensitive, or not sensitive enough, to light, sound, smell, taste or texture.

Many autistic adults have learned to adapt so that the signs are not always noticeable. This is called masking. It can make autism harder to spot, especially in women, who may copy how others behave, seem to cope well socially, and hide their feelings. Men can mask too.
Speak to your GP. They can usually refer you to a local autism team.
A mental health professional may also suggest an assessment if they notice signs.
Waits can be months or longer. Ask your GP what support you can get in the meantime.
In England, the Right to Choose scheme may let you pick an NHS service with a shorter wait.
The assessment may include questionnaires and questions about your early life, relationships, home and work. The team may also speak to someone who knows you well.
Afterwards you get a report covering whether you are autistic, your strengths and any support needs.

Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects attention, energy levels and impulse control. Most people have signs of both types below, but some have only one. Signs usually start before age 12. ADHD is often missed in women, because inattentive signs can be harder to spot.
Finding it hard to manage your time.
Struggling to follow instructions or finish tasks.
Having lots of energy or feeling restless.
Talking a lot or interrupting people.
Making quick decisions without thinking about the consequences.
See your GP if the signs affect your work, studies or relationships. They will consider other possible causes too.
Your GP may refer you to an ADHD specialist, such as a psychiatrist.
The assessment looks at your symptoms, especially in childhood and at school, plus your work, family and health.
Waits can be long. In England, the Right to Choose scheme may let you choose a clinic with a shorter wait.
Treatment can include lifestyle changes, changes at work, medicine and talking therapies such as CBT. Not everyone needs or wants medicine.
Medicine must be started and monitored by an ADHD specialist.
Regular exercise can help manage energy and ease anxiety and low mood.
Keep a regular bedtime and cut down on screens, caffeine, sugar and alcohol before bed.
Eat a balanced diet at regular times.
Talk to friends and family about your ADHD.
You must tell the DVLA if your ADHD or your medicine affects your driving.

Dyslexia is a common learning difficulty where your brain works differently to most people. It mainly affects reading and writing, and can also affect numbers and planning. It does not affect intelligence.
Making lots of spelling mistakes, or mixing up words that look similar.
Needing to read things more than once.
Getting tired quickly when reading or writing.
Finding it hard to tell left from right.
Difficulty managing time, or remembering dates and names.
Many people with dyslexia are strong in other areas but find some everyday tasks harder.
A dyslexia assessment is not done by a medical doctor. It is usually done by an educational psychologist or a dyslexia specialist.
You can arrange one through the British Dyslexia Association or a private service.
Most people have to pay for a diagnostic assessment.
Dyspraxia, also called developmental co-ordination disorder (DCD), mainly affects movement and co-ordination.
Clumsiness, bumping into things or dropping things.
Finding fine tasks like typing or tying shoelaces hard.
Finding it harder to learn new skills, remember information, or plan and organise your time.
See your GP if it affects your life. They may refer you to a specialist such as an occupational therapist.
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy can help.

Dyscalculia is a difficulty with understanding and working with numbers. It can affect things like ordering and comparing numbers, estimating, and place value. How much it affects someone varies from person to person and over their life.
Reasonable adjustments at work or college
Employers, colleges and universities can make changes, called reasonable adjustments, to help you. Telling them about your condition helps them know what support to offer. Examples include:
Written instructions as well as spoken ones.
Extra time for reading and tasks.
Tools such as screen readers, or information in video format.
Access to Work is a government scheme that can pay for practical support at work, such as specialist equipment, help with travel costs, or mental health support.
If you are at college, university or on an apprenticeship, speak to a teacher or learning support officer. After a diagnostic assessment you may be able to apply for Disabled Students' Allowance.
Talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) or mindfulness may be recommended for ADHD and dyspraxia, and can help with anxiety or low mood.

Supporting the families who support those who serve.

Deployment affects the whole family. Many families find it helps to know the emotional phases people often go through. These phases come from a widely used model of the emotional cycle of deployment, not from NHS guidance, and every family's experience is different.

Preparing practically can reduce anxiety:

• Discuss finances — set up joint access, know where important documents are
• Agree on communication expectations — how often, what platforms
• Create a family calendar with key dates
• Set up a support network — friends, family, other service families
• Make a list of emergency contacts (both military and civilian)
• Ensure car, house, and appliance maintenance is sorted
• Take photos together and write letters/cards to open during deployment
• Discuss plans for children's routines and activities

Having a plan reduces the "what ifs" and gives you both confidence.
Making the most of limited contact

Communication may be limited depending on where they are deployed:

• Agree in advance on realistic expectations — they may not be able to call when planned
• Don't assume the worst if you don't hear from them
• Keep conversations positive when possible — they worry about you too
• It's okay to share difficult news, but choose the right moment
• Send emails, photos, and care packages — these mean everything
• If children are involved, help them write letters or draw pictures
• Some deployments have "communication blackouts" — this is normal

Quality matters more than quantity. One good call can sustain you for weeks.
When they come back — what to expect

Homecoming is exciting but can also be challenging:

• Don't expect everything to go back to "normal" immediately
• They may need space and quiet — they've been in a very different environment
• You've both grown and changed — that's okay
• Routines may need renegotiating — you've been running things your way
• Intimacy may feel different at first — be patient with each other
• Children may react unexpectedly — some may be clingy, others distant
• Watch for signs of PTSD or mental health struggles (irritability, nightmares, withdrawal)
• Give it time. Most families find a new rhythm within a few weeks

If readjustment is taking longer than expected, support is available — don't wait to ask.
Military life is unique. Understanding what your partner or family member experiences helps build empathy and connection.
You can't pour from an empty cup. Your wellbeing matters — not just for you, but for your whole family.
Children experience deployment differently depending on their age. Understanding their perspective helps you support them through it.
If you or someone in your family is in immediate danger or having a mental health crisis, call your local emergency number now.

Asking for help is brave, not weak. Here are ways to start:

• "I'm struggling with the deployment and could use some support"
• "I think I need someone to talk to — can you help me find the right service?"
• "My children are finding this hard and I need advice"
• "I'm not coping as well as I thought I would"

You can talk to:
• Your partner's unit welfare officer
• Your GP / doctor
• Any of the organisations listed above
• A trusted friend or family member

You don't have to have all the answers. Just reaching out is the first step.
Anxiety, denial, tension, arguments, emotional distance. It's common to pick fights or withdraw as a way of "preparing" for separation. This is normal.
Talk openly about fears. Make practical plans together. Spend quality time without pressure. Accept that mixed emotions are normal.

Why They Can't Always Talk About It

Your partner may not be able to share details about their work. This isn't about trust — it's about security.

• Operational security (OPSEC) means some information must stay classified
• They may not be able to tell you where they're going or what they're doing
• This can feel like being shut out — but it's designed to protect everyone
• Focus on how they're feeling rather than what they're doing
• If they seem stressed but can't explain why, just being present helps

You don't need to know the details to be supportive. Sometimes "I'm here for you" is enough.
Why they seem different at home

Military culture shapes how people think and behave:

• They're trained to suppress emotions and "crack on" — this doesn't mean they don't feel
• They may struggle to switch off from "work mode" at home
• Dark humour is a coping mechanism — it doesn't mean they don't take things seriously
• They may seem more rigid or controlling — structure is comforting after chaotic environments
• Loyalty to their unit is deep — it's not a replacement for loyalty to family

Understanding the culture helps you not take things personally. It also helps them feel understood.

Military families often relocate every 2–3 years:

• It's okay to grieve the life you're leaving behind each time
• Building a support network quickly is essential — other service families understand
• Children may struggle with changing schools — acknowledge their feelings
• It gets easier to settle in with practice, but it's always a challenge
• Try to find one constant — a hobby, routine, or tradition that travels with you
• Some families choose to stay in one place while the serving member commutes — this is valid too

You are not "just following them around." You are making sacrifices too, and that matters.

Mental health challenges are common in service personnel:

• PTSD, anxiety, depression, and adjustment disorders are all more prevalent
• Many serving members won't seek help due to stigma or fear of career impact
• Signs to watch for: irritability, nightmares, withdrawal, alcohol increase, emotional numbness
• You cannot fix them — but you can encourage them to seek professional help
• Don't take their struggles personally — it's not about you
• Your own mental health is affected by theirs — you need support too

If you're concerned, speak to their welfare officer or one of the support organisations in the "Get Help" tab.

Military social events can feel unfamiliar:

• Mess dinners, families days, and social functions are part of military life
• There may be rank-related social protocols — ask your partner to brief you
• You don't have to attend everything — but showing up sometimes matters to them
• Other military spouses/partners are often the best resource for what to expect
• You are not defined by your partner's rank — you are your own person

Don't worry about getting everything right. Most people are welcoming and understanding.
When the house feels too quiet

Loneliness during deployment is one of the biggest challenges:

• Keep a routine — structure fills the gaps
• Stay connected with friends and family, not just the military community
• Join a class, group, or activity — something that's just for you
• Have a "bad day plan" — a list of things that comfort you (film, walk, call a friend)
• Don't feel guilty for enjoying yourself — life doesn't stop during deployment
• Write a journal or send letters — even if you don't post them

Loneliness is not weakness. It's the natural response to missing someone you love.
You are more than their partner

It's easy to lose yourself in the military lifestyle:

• Pursue your own career, education, or hobbies
• Set goals that are about YOUR life, not just theirs
• Build friendships outside the military bubble
• It's okay to say "this is hard" — you don't have to be endlessly supportive
• Your sacrifices are real and valid — acknowledge them
• Find community with other spouses/partners who understand

A strong relationship needs two whole people — not one person living entirely in the other's world.

It's completely normal to sometimes feel:

• Angry that they "chose" this over being at home
• Resentful about managing everything alone
• Jealous of families who are together
• Frustrated by cancelled leave or extended deployments
• Guilty for feeling any of these things

These are VALID feelings. Having them doesn't make you a bad partner or unsupportive.

What helps:
• Acknowledge the feelings without judgment
• Talk to someone who understands (other military families)
• Don't bottle it up until it explodes
• Remember: you can love someone and still be angry about the situation

Stress and loneliness can affect your physical health:

• Keep moving — even a 20-minute walk makes a difference
• Eat properly — it's tempting to skip meals or comfort eat
• Sleep matters — establish a bedtime routine
• Limit alcohol — it's easy to use it as a coping mechanism
• Don't ignore health appointments — GP, dentist, check-ups
• Base gyms are often available to families — use them if you can

Looking after your body helps your mind cope better too.
I am allowed to find this hard.
I am holding this family together and that takes strength.
Asking for help is brave, not weak.

This is temporary — we will get through it.
Too young to understand, but still affected

Very young children can't understand deployment but they sense changes:

• They may become clingy, fussy, or have sleep disruptions
• Keep routines as consistent as possible
• Use photos and videos to maintain familiarity with the deployed parent
• Play recordings of their voice at bedtime
• Don't force them to interact via video call if they're not interested — they're too young to understand
• Your calm energy helps them feel safe

They won't remember the deployment, but the stability you provide now builds their security foundation.

Children this age know someone is missing but may not understand why:

• Explain simply: "Daddy/Mummy has to go away for work to help keep people safe"
• Use a calendar or countdown chain they can physically interact with
• Let them help pack a care package
• Expect some regression (bedwetting, tantrums, clinginess)
• Don't promise exact return dates — say "when their job is finished"
• Read books about deployment — several are written for this age group
• Reassure frequently: "They love you, they'll come back"

Consistency and reassurance are everything at this age.
They understand more and worry more

This age group understands deployment is potentially dangerous:

• Be honest but age-appropriate — don't lie but don't overload with detail
• Let them express feelings without judgment
• They may act out at school or with friends — this is their way of processing
• Give them a job: "You're in charge of sending photos to Dad/Mum every week"
• Maintain their activities and friendships — stability helps
• Watch for anxiety, sleep changes, or grades dropping
• News and social media can be scary — monitor and discuss what they see

They need to feel involved and valued, not just "managed."
They have their own complex feelings

Teenagers experience deployment through an adult lens:

• They may feel angry, embarrassed, or resentful
• They may take on a "parent" role to help — watch for them overloading
• Give them space but stay available
• Don't expect them to be "the man/woman of the house" — they're still children
• They may worry about the same things you do — danger, infidelity, change
• Social media makes deployment harder — they see other families together
• Let them communicate with the deployed parent independently too

Teenagers need to know they can be honest about how they feel without being told to "be strong."
Maintain routines as much as possible — routine equals safety
Don't hide your emotions entirely — children learn it's okay to feel from watching you
But don't lean on them for emotional support — that's an adult's job
Let them connect with other military children who understand
Mark milestones together — halfway point, one month to go
Create a "deployment box" with letters, photos, and small gifts from the deployed parent
If behaviour changes significantly, speak to their school and your GP
Remind them regularly: they are loved, they are safe, and this is temporary

Common early signs include:

• Missed period — the most common first sign
• Feeling sick or nauseous (morning sickness can happen any time of day)
• Unusual tiredness or fatigue
• Breast tenderness or changes
• Needing to wee more often
• Changes in taste or smell
• Light spotting (implantation bleeding)

If you suspect you may be pregnant, speak to your Medical Officer as soon as possible. This is completely confidential.

You are not required to announce pregnancy publicly. Here's how the process typically works:

• Confirm pregnancy through your Medical Officer (confidential)
• Your MO will conduct a risk assessment for your role
• You will need to inform your line manager — your MO can support you with this
• A workplace risk assessment will be carried out
• Duties may be adjusted to remove physical risks
• You are protected from discrimination under service and civilian law

You cannot be discharged or disadvantaged because of pregnancy. If you feel pressured, speak to your unit welfare officer or the Service Complaints process.

Service personnel are entitled to maternity provisions:

• Up to 52 weeks maternity leave (26 ordinary + 26 additional)
• Maternity pay — similar to civilian statutory maternity pay
• Right to return to your role or equivalent
• Shared Parental Leave may also be available
• Partner may be entitled to paternity leave

Specific entitlements vary by service branch and may be updated. Speak to your unit HR / admin office for the latest policy, or check the relevant Joint Service Publication (JSP).

Staying active during pregnancy is generally encouraged, but with adjustments:

• You will be exempt from standard fitness tests during pregnancy
• Low-impact exercise (walking, swimming, yoga) is usually safe
• Avoid contact sports, heavy lifting, and high-impact activities
• Stop immediately if you experience pain, dizziness, or bleeding
• Your MO will provide specific guidance based on your role and stage of pregnancy

After birth, there is a graduated return to fitness. You won't be expected to pass fitness tests immediately. Your MO will set a realistic timeline.

Once pregnancy is confirmed:

• You will not be deployed to operational theatres
• Travel restrictions apply — especially after 28 weeks (air travel)
• You may continue in your normal role with adjustments, depending on the risk assessment
• Desk-based or rear-party duties are typical
• If you discover you are pregnant while deployed, inform your MO immediately for safe extraction planning

Your safety and the baby's safety are the priority. No one should pressure you to hide pregnancy to maintain deployment.

Planning your return:

• You have the right to return to your role or an equivalent position
• Graduated return to physical fitness — no rush
• Childcare support may be available — check your service's family support
• Breastfeeding arrangements — your unit should provide private space and time
• Mental health support is available if you experience postnatal depression or anxiety
• Flexible working arrangements may be possible depending on your role

Many service women successfully balance military careers with parenthood. Speak to other service mothers and your welfare team for practical advice.

Pregnancy loss (miscarriage, stillbirth, or ectopic pregnancy) is more common than many people realise. You are not alone.

• Seek immediate medical help if you experience heavy bleeding, severe pain, or feel unwell
• Your Medical Officer is there to support you — this is confidential
• You are entitled to compassionate leave
• Counselling support is available through military mental health services
• Your chain of command should be supportive — if they are not, speak to your welfare officer
• Partners also need support — they can access help too

There is no "right way" to grieve. Take the time you need. You can also reach out to charities like Tommy's and the Miscarriage Association for additional support.

In England you can call 111 and choose the mental health option (option 2 in most areas) if you need urgent help but are not in immediate danger. You can call for yourself or for someone else.

If your life is at risk, call 999 or go to A&E. Tell them honestly that you are feeling suicidal and what has happened. Arriving by ambulance does not mean you are seen faster: people are seen in order of how urgent their needs are.
At A&E you register at reception and give basic details, including why you have come.
A doctor or nurse checks how urgently you need care. This is called triage.
Any physical injuries, such as from self-harm or an overdose, are treated.
You will usually be seen by a mental health team. In many hospitals this is the liaison psychiatry team. They will talk with you to understand what is going on and what help you need.
They will ask how you are feeling, and may ask about your physical health.
They may ask what support you have in your life and whether you feel safe at home.
It helps to be honest about your thoughts and any risk to yourself.
Tell them about any medicines, other health conditions, therapy and any crisis plan you have.
You can ask questions, and ask for information in a format or language you understand.
Going to A&E does not automatically mean you will be kept in hospital. Most people get support at home. Depending on the assessment, you might:
Be referred to a crisis team (crisis resolution and home treatment team), who support you at home.
Be asked to see your GP, who will be told about your visit.
Be given self-care advice, and sometimes medication, to take home.
Be sent to another service in the hospital, such as a mental health crisis centre.
Be admitted to hospital if you are seriously unwell.
You might get more than one of these. For example, after a suicide attempt you could be treated on a ward for your injuries and then referred to a crisis team.
If you need to stay in hospital

Sometimes a person can be kept in hospital under the Mental Health Act ("sectioned") if it is needed to keep them or others safe. There are strict rules for this, and staff should explain why.
You cannot be turned away before a medical professional has assessed you.
You should not be sent home without follow-up support.
Staff should ask your permission before sharing your information, unless they are worried about your safety.
You should be treated with kindness and dignity.

Your body goes through many changes during puberty — usually starting between the ages of 8 and 14. Every person develops at their own pace. There is no "normal" timeline.
Puberty for boys usually starts between ages 9 and 14. Changes happen gradually and everyone develops differently. There's no rush.
Excellent! You really know your stuff.

Not bad! Learning is what this is all about.
Now you know more than before — and that's what matters!
The more you learn about your body, the better you can look after yourself. Knowledge is power.
What they are and what to expect

A period is the monthly shedding of the lining of the uterus (womb). It's a completely normal part of the female body's reproductive cycle.

• Periods usually start between ages 10–16 (average is 12)
• A typical period lasts 3–7 days
• You may lose around 30–70ml of blood (less than you think)
• Periods come roughly every 21–35 days
• It's normal for periods to be irregular for the first couple of years
• Products: pads, tampons, menstrual cups, period pants — all are valid choices

Cramps, mood changes, and tiredness are common. Light exercise, a warm water bottle, and rest can help.
Typical cycle: 21–35 days. First periods are often irregular — this is normal.

Breast development is usually one of the first signs of puberty in girls.

• Development typically starts between ages 8–13
• It's normal for breasts to develop at different rates (one may be slightly larger)
• Development can take 3–5 years to complete
• Breast size is genetic — it doesn't affect health or ability
• Tenderness or soreness during development is normal
• Wearing a supportive bra/sports bra can help with comfort during exercise

Every body is different. Comparison to others is not helpful — your body is developing exactly as it should for you.
Development starts age 8–13 and continues for several years.

During puberty, hormonal changes cause new hair growth and skin changes.

• Hair grows under arms, on legs, and in the pubic area
• This is completely normal and natural
• Shaving/not shaving is a personal choice — neither is "wrong"
• Skin may become oilier — this can lead to spots or acne
• Washing your face twice daily with a gentle cleanser can help
• Sweating increases — deodorant/antiperspirant becomes useful

Acne affects most teenagers to some degree. If it's severe or affecting your confidence, speak to a GP — treatments are available.
Acne peaks between ages 14–17 for most people.

During puberty, your body goes through a growth spurt and changes shape.

• Height increases — girls often have their growth spurt earlier than boys (around 10–14)
• Hips may widen — this is part of normal female development
• Body fat increases, particularly around hips, thighs, and buttocks
• Weight gain during puberty is normal and healthy
• Hands and feet may grow first, before the rest of the body catches up

Your body shape is determined by genetics. "Healthy" looks different on everyone. Focus on how you feel, not how you compare to others or images on social media.

Hormonal changes during puberty don't just affect your body — they affect your brain and emotions too.

• Mood swings are common and normal
• You may feel more emotional, irritable, or sensitive
• Crushes and new feelings about attraction are normal
• Feeling self-conscious about your changing body is very common
• Wanting more privacy and independence is a healthy sign of growing up

These feelings are caused by hormones (mainly oestrogen and progesterone). They won't always feel this intense. Talking to someone you trust can help a lot.
Hormonal mood changes typically settle as you move through your late teens.

Vaginal discharge is normal and a sign that your body is working properly.

• Discharge usually starts 6–12 months before your first period
• Normal discharge is clear or white and doesn't have a strong odour
• The amount and texture changes throughout your cycle
• The vagina is self-cleaning — you don't need special products inside it
• Wash the external area (vulva) with warm water and mild, unperfumed soap
• Wearing breathable cotton underwear helps

See a doctor if discharge changes colour (green/grey), has a strong smell, or if you have itching or pain.
Discharge starting around ages 10–12 is usually the first sign puberty has begun.

During puberty, the larynx (voice box) grows larger, causing the voice to deepen.

• Your voice may "crack" or squeak during the transition — this is normal
• The Adam's apple (bump in the throat) becomes more noticeable
• Voice deepening usually happens between ages 12–16
• The transition can take several months to complete
• Everyone's voice deepens at a different rate

Voice cracking can feel embarrassing, but it happens to everyone. It's temporary and will settle.
Voice typically finishes deepening by age 16–17.

Boys typically have their main growth spurt between ages 12–16.

• You may grow several inches in a short time
• Shoulders broaden and muscles develop
• Hands and feet often grow first — you may feel "clumsy" temporarily
• Growing pains (aches in legs) are common during growth spurts
• Good nutrition and sleep are essential for healthy growth
• Muscle development continues into your early 20s

Don't compare your growth to others. Some people develop earlier or later. Genetics play a major role in your final height and build.
Most boys reach adult height between ages 16–18, some continue growing until 21.

Increased testosterone during puberty causes hair to grow in new places.

• Pubic hair is usually the first new hair to appear
• Underarm hair, leg hair, and chest hair follow
• Facial hair (upper lip first, then chin and cheeks) often starts around 14–16
• Full beard growth may not happen until your late teens or 20s
• The amount and thickness of body hair is genetic
• Shaving is a personal choice — there's no "right" time to start

If you choose to shave, use a clean razor and shaving cream to avoid irritation.
Facial hair can continue filling in well into your 20s.

Rising testosterone levels increase oil production in your skin.

• Oily skin and acne (spots) are very common during puberty
• Face, back, chest, and shoulders are most affected
• Wash affected areas twice daily with a gentle cleanser
• Don't squeeze spots — this can cause scarring and infection
• Drinking water and eating well can help your skin
• Sweating increases — daily showers and deodorant become important

Acne is not caused by poor hygiene or diet alone — it's primarily hormonal. If it's severe, a GP can prescribe treatments.
Acne is very common during the teenage years. If it is bothering you or leaving scars, a pharmacist or GP can help.

During puberty, the reproductive system matures.

• Testicles grow larger (usually the first sign of puberty)
• The penis grows in both length and width
• Erections happen more frequently — sometimes without reason (this is normal)
• Wet dreams (nocturnal emissions) may occur — this is completely normal
• These changes are driven by testosterone
• Everyone develops at a different rate — size and development varies enormously

These changes can feel awkward or embarrassing, but they are a normal part of growing up. Every male goes through them.

Testosterone changes don't just affect your body — they affect your mood and emotions too.

• You may feel more irritable or frustrated
• Mood swings and sudden anger are common
• New feelings about attraction and relationships emerge
• Feeling self-conscious about your body is very normal
• Pressure to "man up" or hide feelings is harmful — emotions are healthy
• Risk-taking behaviour may increase — be aware of this

It's okay to feel things strongly. Talking to someone — a parent, teacher, counsellor, or friend — is a sign of strength, not weakness.
Hormonal mood changes typically stabilise in your late teens.
You can't get pregnant on your first time having sex.
This is a myth. Pregnancy can occur any time unprotected sex happens, including the first time. Contraception should always be used to prevent unintended pregnancy.
Periods can be irregular for the first few years after they start.
This is a fact. It's very common for periods to be unpredictable in the first 1–2 years. The cycle usually becomes more regular as you get older.
Shaving makes hair grow back thicker.
This is a myth. Shaving cuts hair at the surface, creating a blunt edge that can feel stubbly. But the hair itself doesn't actually become thicker or darker.
Boys go through puberty too — including mood swings and emotional changes.

This is a fact. Testosterone causes significant emotional changes in boys during puberty, including mood swings, irritability, and new feelings. Boys are often told to hide these feelings, but that's not healthy.
Acne is caused by not washing your face enough.
This is a myth. Acne is primarily caused by hormonal changes during puberty, not dirt. Over-washing can actually make acne worse by irritating the skin. Gentle, twice-daily cleansing is recommended.
Wet dreams are a normal part of male puberty.
This is a fact. Nocturnal emissions (wet dreams) are a completely normal part of puberty. They happen because the body is producing more hormones. Nothing to be embarrassed about.
Everyone goes through puberty at the same age.
This is a myth. The NHS says puberty usually starts between the ages of 8 and 14, depending on genetics and other factors. Starting earlier or later than friends is completely normal.
Vaginal discharge before periods start is normal.
This is a fact. Clear or white discharge usually begins 6–12 months before the first period. It's a sign that puberty is progressing normally.
You should use scented products to clean the vaginal area.
This is a myth. The vagina is self-cleaning. Scented products can disrupt the natural pH balance and cause irritation or infections. Warm water and mild, unperfumed soap on the external area is best.
Mood swings during puberty are caused by hormonal changes in the brain.
This is a fact. Hormones like oestrogen, progesterone, and testosterone directly affect the brain during puberty, causing mood changes, stronger emotions, and shifts in how you feel day to day.
If a boy hasn't started puberty by 14, something is wrong.
This is a myth. While most boys start puberty between 9–14, some start later and that's still within the normal range. If concerned, a GP can check — but later development is usually just genetics.
Exercise can help with period cramps.
This is a fact. Light to moderate exercise releases endorphins (natural painkillers) that can help reduce menstrual cramps. Walking, yoga, and swimming are particularly helpful.

• Many acts shown in porn are not things most people do or enjoy

Sending or receiving sexual images is a serious matter, especially for under-18s:

• Taking, sending, or possessing sexual images of under-18s is illegal — even your own images
• Once an image is sent, you lose all control over where it goes
• Images can be shared, screenshotted, or used for blackmail
• "Revenge porn" (sharing intimate images without consent) is a criminal offence
• If someone pressures you for images, that is coercion — tell a trusted adult
• If an image of you has been shared, you can report it to police or CEOP

Never send an image you wouldn't want your family, school, or future employer to see.

Sexuality and gender identity are natural parts of who you are:

• Sexual orientation (who you're attracted to) exists on a spectrum
• Common terms: straight, gay, lesbian, bisexual, asexual, pansexual — and more
• Gender identity (how you feel inside) may or may not match the sex you were assigned at birth
• It's normal to question or explore your identity — there's no deadline
• You don't have to label yourself if you don't want to
• Coming out is a personal choice — only do it when you feel safe and ready

Everyone deserves to be treated with respect regardless of their identity. Discrimination and bullying based on sexuality or gender is never acceptable.

If you need advice, support, or are worried about anything:

• Your GP / Doctor — completely confidential, even for under-16s
• Sexual health clinics — free, confidential testing and advice
• School nurse or counsellor
• Childline — free, confidential support for under-19s (available online)
• Brook — sexual health charity for young people (brook.org.uk)
• The Mix — support for under-25s (themix.org.uk)

Asking for help or information is a sign of maturity, not weakness. No question is too embarrassing.
